fixes.name: deployment.rollback-to-revision
fixes.description: Roll the Deployment back to the pod template of an earlier revision, as kubectl rollout undo does. revision is that revision's number, from the rollout history.
fixes.params_schema: {"type":"object","additionalProperties":false,"required":["revision"],"properties":{"revision":{"type":"integer","minimum":1,"description":"The earlier revision to roll back to."}}}

fixes.name: deployment.set-resources
fixes.description: Set the memory and CPU requests and limits of containers in the Deployment's pod template, which rolls out new pods. containers maps each container's name to the requests and limits to set, as Kubernetes quantities such as 512Mi or 250m; values not named stay as they are. Choose the values from the evidence: Themis checks that they are valid and that the cluster can run them, never how big they are. A limit can't be removed, and a request can't end above its limit.

fixes.name: deployment.set-probes
fixes.description: Change the timing of a container's existing liveness, readiness or startup probes: initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds, failureThreshold, and successThreshold for readiness. Give only the fields to change, with the values the evidence supports. It can't add or remove a probe, or change what the probe calls.

root_causes.name: new_version_broken
root_causes.description: a recent rollout brought a version that fails, where the one before it worked

guidance:
From the rollout-regression profile, which offers deployment.rollback-to-revision:
A rollback is right when the latest rollout brought the failures: it
changed what the pods run (rollout_changed_the_app is true), and the
revision before it does better, running without failing beside the
failing pods, or using clearly less of its memory limit at the same age
(failures_came_with_rollout is true). If the rollout changed only labels
or annotations, such as a restart, if the failure started before the
rollout, if there is no earlier revision or it failed too, if the
current revision uses no more of its limit than the one before it did
at the same age or by its end, so demand grew (failures_came_with_rollout
is false), if the target is managed by GitOps, if its config changed
before the failure, or if the evidence is missing, such as no history of
the revision before it (failures_came_with_rollout is unknown), do not
propose a rollback: conclude inconclusive and say what is missing.

When oom_killed_new_revision, failure_onset_after_rollout and
failures_came_with_rollout are all true, and gitops_managed and
config_changed_before_failure are false, rolling back to the revision
before it is justified, even if the logs are empty: a process killed for
memory often writes nothing.

Naming a cause doesn't make a rollback right: these conditions do.

From the oom-limit-too-low profile, which offers deployment.set-resources:
Raising a container's memory limit is right when containers are killed
for memory and need more than their limit, and the latest rollout didn't
bring the kills: oom_killed_current_revision is true,
failures_came_with_rollout is false, memory_at_limit_before_kill is true,
or unknown without peak figures, and nothing below applies.
failures_came_with_rollout is false when there is no earlier version to
go back to, when the one before it failed too, when the rollout changed
nothing the pods run, only labels or annotations, as a restart does, or
when this version uses no more of its memory limit than the one before
it did at the same age, or than it had come to use by its end: what
changed since, such as more data or load, brought the kills. Without
memory figures of both versions, it is false when this one ran without
failing at least as long as the one before it did. Raise the
memory limit of the killed containers only, citing pod_states, and
container_memory when it has figures. Size it from the evidence: the
peak plus 25% when container_memory shows it, otherwise 1.5 times the
current limit. Never lower a value, never change CPU, never set a limit
where there was none, and never remove one.

Missing peak memory figures are no reason to decline: OOM kills in the
pod states are enough to act on. They only mean the size can't come from
the peak.

Don't raise it, and say what you found instead, when:
- failures_came_with_rollout is true: the rollout changed what the pods
  run, and the version before this one ran without failing where this
  one fails, or used clearly less of its limit at the same age, so this
  one brought the kills.
  Whether to roll it back is a rollback's question, under its own
  guidance, never a reason to raise the limit here.
- failures_came_with_rollout is unknown: nothing shows how the version
  before this one ran, such as no metrics history of its pods. Neither
  fix is justified; say what is missing.
- oom_after_long_run is true, the containers are killed again and again
  after hours of running, and the limit held for days before: memory
  that grows until the container is killed, at any limit. A higher limit
  only delays the next kill; say so and leave it to a person.
- memory_at_limit_before_kill is false: the containers never came near
  their limit, so the limit isn't what killed them.
- evicted_for_node_memory is true: the node ran short of memory. A
  higher limit doesn't give it more, and can make it worse.
- oom_killed_current_revision is not true: a container killed with exit
  code 137 and no OOMKilled reason may have been stopped for another
  reason. Don't infer a memory kill from restarts, exit codes or the
  alert alone; say what is missing.

From the probe-restart-storm profile, which offers deployment.set-probes:
Changing a probe's timing is right when the application works and the
probe fails it only because it is slower than the probe allows: it is
killed while still starting (killed_during_startup), or its probes time
out (probe_timeouts) on answers that come a little after the probe's
timeout. The logs then show it starting or serving normally until it is
stopped, and crashed_on_its_own is false. Each revision's probe timings
are in the rollout history: compare them with how long containers ran and
with the probe failure messages.

Decide which probes to change and to what, from that evidence: liveness,
readiness or startup, and initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds,
timeoutSeconds, failureThreshold or, for readiness, successThreshold.
Give the values the evidence supports, such as a timeout above the
answers' latency, or enough delay or failures to cover the start the logs
show, and cite them. A readiness probe made more lenient keeps sending
traffic to pods that fail it for longer: change it only when the
evidence shows readiness failing a pod that serves.

Don't change a probe, and say what you found instead, when:
- the application is failing: errors or stack traces in the logs,
  crashed_on_its_own is true, or probes get error answers from a
  container that is up. A probe failing is then a symptom.
- the latest rollout changed what the pods run and brought the failures,
  where the revision before it ran without failing
  (failures_came_with_rollout is true): whether to
  roll back is another kind of incident's call, unless the logs show the
  new version only starts slower.
- something the application calls is down, and its readiness probe says
  so: a more lenient probe would send traffic to pods that can't serve
  it, and hide the outage.
- probe_kills and probe_timeouts are both false: nothing shows the probes
  failing a container that works.

templates.name: rollout_history
templates.description: The Deployment's rollout progress, conditions, GitOps ownership markers, each ReplicaSet revision with its images and resource limits, and what the current revision changed from the one before it: in what its pods run, or only in their labels and annotations.

templates.name: pod_states
templates.description: Each pod of the Deployment: its revision, readiness, and each container's state and last termination (where OOMKilled shows).

templates.name: target_events
templates.description: Recent events of the Deployment, its ReplicaSets and its pods, newest first.

templates.name: referenced_config
templates.description: The ConfigMaps and Secrets the pod template refers to, and when each ConfigMap last changed. Names and times only, never values.

templates.name: container_logs_tail
templates.description: The end of one container's logs. Defaults to the pod needing attention most, from the run that last ended.

templates.name: revision_health
templates.description: How the pods of the current revision and of the one before it ran, from the metrics source's history: when it first and last has them, their restarts and OOM kills, and their CPU throttling, each with when it first showed; and how much of its memory and CPU limits each container used on average, over the same time since each revision started, and for the one before, over its last that long. A source without history says so.

gaps.detail: collect revision_health: no figures: no metrics source is set up

predicates.reason: 3 pods of revision 3 are ready and never failed

predicates.name: rollout_changed_the_app
predicates.reason: revision 4 changed what its pods run (the image of container app changed from example/api-gateway:1.19.4 to example/api-gateway:1.20.0)

predicates.name: failures_came_with_rollout
predicates.reason: revision 4 changed what its pods run (the image of container app changed from example/api-gateway:1.19.4 to example/api-gateway:1.20.0), and 3 pods of revision 3 run without failing while revision 4 fails

predicates.name: oom_killed_new_revision
predicates.reason: none of the 1 pods of revision 4 was OOMKilled

predicates.name: config_changed_before_failure
predicates.reason: no referenced ConfigMap changed between the rollout and the first failure

predicates.name: oom_killed_current_revision
predicates.reason: none of the 1 pods of revision 4 was OOMKilled

predicates.name: oom_after_long_run
predicates.reason: no container of revision 4 was OOMKilled

predicates.name: evicted_for_node_memory
predicates.reason: no pod was evicted for its node's memory

predicates.reason: api-gateway-9d4e1c6a3-q6w2e/app ran 1m2s before it was stopped, as soon as its liveness probe could fail it: it never passed the probe

predicates.reason: no container ended with an error or ran out of memory; any that ended were stopped

policy.reason: Policy rule rollback-needs-approval of the rollout-regression profile requires a person's approval.

unproposed: The checks support a rollback (the failures started after the rollout) and a probe change (the kubelet restarts a container because its liveness or startup probe fails).
